extracted.intended_audience: academics, journal editors, students and general readers interested in academic publishing, scholarly ethics, and science-and-society debates
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the editorial and ethical standards of academic journals (peer review, use of expertise, evidence and argument quality, and avoidance of ideological bias) as illustrated by the Sokal affair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of academic peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Social Text did not practice academic peer review at the time and therefore did not submit the article for outside expert review by a physicist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For submissions that touch on technical or specialist subjects, journals should seek outside expert peer review; publishing without peer review is an anti-pattern when technical accuracy or domain expertise is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual/editorial rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sokal experiment was explicitly intended to 'test the journal's intellectual rigor' — whether editors analyze the quality of evidence, cogency of arguments, and relevance of arguments to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should evaluate submissions for logical coherence, evidentiary support, and relevance to stated claims; accepting pieces that 'sound good' but lack substantive support indicates low editorial rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of evidence and cogency of arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sokal argued editors 'felt no need to analyze the quality of the evidence, the cogency of the arguments, or even the relevance of the arguments to the purported conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claims are supported by appropriate evidence and clear reasoning; an article that asserts conclusions without evidence or cogent argumentation should be revised or rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation of appropriate disciplinary expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Social Text 'felt comfortable publishing an article on quantum physics without bothering to consult anyone knowledgeable in the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a submission intersects another discipline (e.g., humanities piece making scientific claims), editors should solicit review or advice from specialists in the relevant field to check for basic factual and conceptual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ideological bias / confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Sokal suspected the article would be published if it 'flattered the editors' ideological preconceptions.' Hilgartner noted audiences may apply less stringent standards to targets they view unfavorably (confirmational bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should guard against accepting work primarily because it aligns with editors' political/ideological positions; apply consistent evidentiary and ethical standards regardless of whether the work confirms or challenges editors' views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conduct in submissions and hoaxing
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether Sokal was wrong to deceive the editors or readers by submitting a deliberately bogus article; Social Text's editors accused Sokal of unethical behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While exposing editorial weakness may have scholarly interest, deliberate deception of editors/readers raises ethical questions; consider transparency and the ethics of sting operations when evaluating such interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and quality of writing; responsiveness to editorial revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors noted concerns about the quality of the writing and requested changes (to excise philosophical speculation and many footnotes); they described Sokal as 'difficult, uncooperative' for refusing some changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly written or obscure prose should trigger editorial revision requests; authors' willingness to make substantive edits and respond constructively to editorial feedback is a marker of professional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of scientific terminology and conceptual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sokal and Bricmont later criticized extracts from intellectuals for misusing scientific terminology; the hoax's content conflated scientific concepts with sociopolitical rhetoric (e.g., claiming physical reality is 'a social and linguistic construct').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating technical scientific terms with metaphorical or political language; ensure scientific concepts are used accurately and not merely as rhetorical ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to journal scope and declared disciplinary contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Social Text defended not seeking peer review by saying the article was not offered as a contribution to physics and that the journal was one of open intellectual inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a submission falls within a journal's scope; if a piece purports to make disciplinary claims (e.g., scientific claims), that should be made explicit and treated accordingly (including seeking appropriate reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority/credential effects on editorial decisions (status bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sokal observed the article was published partly 'because an academic authority had written it' — illustrating how author credentials can influence editorial acceptance (related to the 'Dr. Fox effect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be cautious of letting author reputation substitute for content evaluation; implement blind review or other safeguards when possible to mitigate status-driven bias.
